mappings.note: Identifies methanoic acid from litmus and the carbonate effervescence. LO-8 names only ethanoic acid, so the outcome is a homologue short of the compound examined; cited anyway because the tested chemistry is exactly the carboxylic-acid behaviour LO-8 describes.
Chemical discrimination of an alcohol from a carboxylic acid by litmus and bicarbonate - a direct contrast of the two compounds LO-8 names.
Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester, named as saponification in LO-8. LO-9 is not cited because the soap's cleansing behaviour is not in question.
Two tests for the acidity of acetic acid - properties of ethanoic acid, LO-8.
Advantages of detergents set against their environmental harm - the soaps-versus-detergents clause of LO-9.
Observation for alkaline KMnO4 with warm ethanol (decolourisation) - the ethanol oxidation of LO-8, asked observationally.
Chromic anhydride with ethanol giving ethanal. An oxidation of ethanol, so LO-8, although the product named in the outcome is ethanoic acid.

Three parts: fermentation and the ethanol smell sit with LO-8 (as a preparation, imperfectly), but part (c) asks for fractional distillation as the separation method, and distillation is named in the C 1.2 competency itself - the one place in this frame where the competency's separation content is genuinely examined.
Ethanol identified from its use as a skin steriliser and oxidised to ethanoic acid - both the identification and the reaction are LO-8.

Ethanol identified from antifreeze behaviour, with equations for its formation from ethene and for its combustion. The combustion and physical properties are LO-8; the formation half is a preparation the frame does not cover.
Identifies ethanol and ethanoic acid from antifreeze use and the baking-soda test (LO-8), then explicitly demands both structural formulae (C 1.3-LO-4).
Physical properties of ethanol (colour, boiling point, miscibility) - 'describes the properties of ethanol' word for word.
How detergents are made biodegradable (linear chains) - a detergent property under LO-9, the only code covering detergents.
Combustion of ethanol with its equation. Mapped on the named compound (LO-8), following the same rule as sha 3e42dff90bb76abf; generic combustion items go to C 1.3.
Why soap fails in hard water - scum with Ca and Mg ions, the basis of the soap/detergent distinction in LO-9.
Laboratory preparation of soap from oil and NaOH with salting out. Manufacture, so LO-8 (saponification) under the family split; LO-9 is reserved for how the soap then behaves.
Disadvantage of detergents (non-biodegradable) - the soaps-versus-detergents comparison of LO-9.

POOR FIT. Names four washing-powder additives (CMC, sodium carbonate, sodium sulphate, sodium perborate). LO-9 covers cleansing action and the soap/detergent distinction, not commercial formulation; no better code exists and none of the chemistry is in the frame.
Name and structural formula of methanoic acid: naming a carboxylic-acid series member (C 1.1-LO-4) plus the structure (C 1.3-LO-4). Not LO-8, which names only ethanoic acid, and no property is asked.
Ethanol in wine, oxidised by acidified dichromate to ethanoic acid, which then reacts with sodium - a chain of three LO-8 properties.
Observation and product for alkaline KMnO4 added to warm ethanol - the same LO-8 oxidation as sha c7256fa215fdb5f3.

OFF-CHAPTER CONTENT: calcium carbonate with dilute HCl and the lime-water test - inorganic carbonate chemistry from the acids-bases-salts chapter, not carbon compounds. C 1.3 is nevertheless a true fit, since its competency names acid-base reactions and the item demands balanced equations.

Neutralisation and esterification of ethanoic acid (LO-8) plus a demand to name its functional group (C 1.1-LO-4). QUESTION-SIDE DEFECT: compound A is printed as C2H6O but the answer requires C2H4O2 (ethanoic acid); as printed, A and B carry the same formula.

Three separate demands and three codes: dehydration of ethanol with the role of conc. H2SO4 (LO-8), the electron dot structure of the ethene formed (C 1.3-LO-4), and hydrogenation with its industrial role (C 1.3, since addition reactions have no outcome).
Why carbon's bonds are strong and its compounds stable - the small-size and four-valence-electron argument that LO-3 is built on.
